chapters.summary: Forming and modifying the opinion (SA 700, 705), Key Audit Matters (SA 701), Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter paragraphs (SA 706), comparatives (SA 710), other information (SA 720) and reporting under CARO 2020.
chapters.applicableFor: May 2027 onward (ICAI new scheme, CA Final Paper 3)
chapters.lawAsOf: SA 700, 701, 705, 706, 710 and 720 as issued by ICAI; Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 as notified by MCA (no replacement order found as of November 2026)

lesson.heading: SA 700 and SA 705: the opinion
lesson.body:
The auditor forms an opinion on whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework. Under SA 700 the report has the Opinion section first, then Basis for Opinion, then (where applicable) Going Concern, Key Audit Matters, Other Information, Responsibilities of Management and TCWG, Auditor's Responsibilities, and Report on Other Legal and Regulatory Requirements (section 143(3), Rule 11 and CARO).

SA 705 decision matrix:

| Nature of the matter | Material but not pervasive | Material and pervasive |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Financial statements are materially misstated | Qualified opinion | Adverse opinion |
| Unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence | Qualified opinion | Disclaimer of opinion |

**Pervasive** effects are not confined to specific elements, or if confined represent a substantial proportion of the financial statements, or relate to disclosures fundamental to users' understanding.

If a scope limitation is imposed by management after acceptance and is likely to lead to a disclaimer, the auditor requests removal; if refused, communicates with TCWG and considers withdrawal where practicable and permitted by law. A statutory auditor of a company cannot simply withdraw; resignation needs Form ADT-3 under section 140(2).

lesson.heading: SA 701, SA 706, SA 710 and SA 720
lesson.body:
**SA 701 Key Audit Matters (KAM)**: matters of most significance in the audit of the current period, selected from matters communicated to TCWG. Mandatory for audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of **listed entities**, and when the auditor otherwise decides or is required by law.

- A KAM is not a substitute for a modified opinion or a MURGC section.
- A matter giving rise to a qualified or adverse opinion, and a material uncertainty on going concern, are KAMs by nature but are reported in their own sections, with a reference in the KAM section.
- When disclaiming an opinion, the auditor does not communicate KAMs (unless required by law).

**SA 706**:

| Paragraph | Used when |
| --- | --- |
| Emphasis of Matter (EOM) | A matter appropriately presented or disclosed is of fundamental importance to users' understanding (e.g. a major catastrophe, early adoption of a new standard, uncertainty about litigation) |
| Other Matter (OM) | A matter not presented in the financial statements is relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the report (e.g. prior year audited by another auditor, use of other auditors' work) |

An EOM is not used where the matter is a KAM; it does not modify the opinion.

**SA 710**: under the corresponding figures approach (used in India for companies), the opinion refers to the current period only. If the prior-period report was modified and the matter is unresolved, the current opinion is also modified. Under the comparative financial statements approach, the opinion covers each period presented.

**SA 720**: the auditor reads the **other information** in the annual report (Board's report, chairman's statement) and considers material inconsistency with the financial statements or with the auditor's knowledge. The report has a section 'Information Other than the Financial Statements and Auditor's Report Thereon'. If an uncorrected material misstatement of other information exists, the auditor describes it there.

lesson.heading: CARO 2020: applicability
lesson.body:
CARO 2020 applies to every company, including a foreign company, **except**:

- A banking company.
- An insurance company.
- A company licensed to operate under section 8.
- A one person company and a small company (as defined in section 2(85), read with the thresholds currently prescribed).
- A private limited company, not a subsidiary or holding company of a public company, with paid-up capital and reserves and surplus not more than ₹1 crore as on the balance sheet date, total borrowings from any bank or financial institution not more than ₹1 crore at any time during the year, and total revenue (including revenue from discontinued operations) not more than ₹10 crore during the year.

CARO 2020 does not apply to the auditor's report on **consolidated** financial statements, except clause (xxi).

Where the answer to a clause is unfavourable or qualified, the auditor states the reasons.

lesson.heading: CARO 2020: selected clauses of paragraph 3
lesson.body:
| Clause | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| (i) | Property, plant and equipment: records, physical verification, title deeds of immovable property, revaluation, benami proceedings |
| (ii) | Inventory physical verification; discrepancies of 10% or more in aggregate per class; quarterly returns to banks for working capital limits above ₹5 crore secured on current assets agreeing with books |
| (iii) | Investments, guarantees, security, loans and advances to companies, firms, LLPs or other parties |
| (iv) | Compliance with sections 185 and 186 |
| (v) | Deposits and deemed deposits |
| (vi) | Cost records under section 148(1) |
| (vii) | Statutory dues: regular deposit; arrears over six months; disputed dues |
| (viii) | Unrecorded income surrendered or disclosed in tax assessments |
| (ix) | Default in repayment of loans; wilful defaulter; diversion of term loans; short-term funds used for long-term purposes |
| (x) | Money raised by IPO or FPO; preferential allotment or private placement |
| (xi) | Fraud noticed; ADT-4 filing; whistle-blower complaints |
| (xii) | Nidhi company compliance |
| (xiii) | Related party transactions: sections 177 and 188 |
| (xiv) | Internal audit system and consideration of internal audit reports |
| (xv) | Non-cash transactions with directors (section 192) |
| (xvi) | Registration under section 45-IA of the RBI Act; CIC matters |
| (xvii) | Cash losses in the year and the immediately preceding year |
| (xviii) | Resignation of statutory auditors |
| (xix) | Material uncertainty on meeting liabilities within one year, based on ratios, ageing and plans |
| (xx) | Unspent CSR amounts and transfer to a Schedule VII fund or the Unspent CSR Account |
| (xxi) | Qualifications or adverse remarks in CARO reports of companies included in consolidated financial statements |

keyPoints: SA 705: misstatement material = qualified; material and pervasive = adverse; scope limitation material = qualified; pervasive = disclaimer.
SA 701: KAM mandatory for listed entities; not a substitute for modification; no KAM when disclaiming.
SA 706: EOM for matters disclosed and fundamental; OM for matters not in the financial statements.
SA 710: corresponding figures approach, opinion refers to current period only.
CARO 2020 excludes banking, insurance, section 8, OPC, small companies and small private companies (₹1 crore / ₹1 crore / ₹10 crore tests).
CARO 2020 does not apply to CFS except clause (xxi); clause (xvii) cash losses, (xviii) auditor resignation, (xix) meeting liabilities, (xx) unspent CSR.

cases.title: Case: Lotus Foods Ltd
cases.body:
Lotus Foods Ltd is listed on BSE. Overall materiality for FY 2025-26 is ₹1.5 crore; profit before tax is ₹28 crore.

| Item | Fact |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory | Slow-moving inventory needs a write-down of ₹3.2 crore as per the auditor's evidence; management refuses to record it. No other misstatements. |
| Revenue | Revenue recognition involving rebates to distributors required significant auditor attention and was discussed with the audit committee |
| Flood | A flood in July 2025 damaged a plant; the loss is properly accounted and disclosed in Note 34 |
| CSR | ₹1.1 crore of CSR obligation for an ongoing project remained unspent at year end |
| Cash | The company had no cash losses in FY 2025-26 or FY 2024-25 |
| Annual report | The Board's report states 'all inventory is valued at cost', which is inconsistent with Note 2 on lower of cost and NRV |

questions.prompt: The auditor could not attend the inventory count or apply alternative procedures. Inventory is 60% of total assets and affects cost of sales and profit substantially. The appropriate opinion is:
options: Unmodified opinion with Emphasis of Matter
questions.explanation: This is an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence, and its possible effects are material and pervasive (a substantial proportion of the financial statements), so SA 705 requires a disclaimer.

questions.prompt: Under SA 701, communicating Key Audit Matters is mandatory for:
options: Audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities
Only when the opinion is modified
questions.explanation: SA 701 applies to listed entities, and to other entities where the auditor decides to communicate KAMs or law or regulation requires it.

questions.prompt: Which of the following companies is covered by CARO 2020?
options: A private company that is a subsidiary of a public company, with revenue of ₹6 crore
questions.explanation: The small private company exemption is not available to a private company that is a holding or subsidiary of a public company, so this company is covered. The other three are expressly excluded.

questions.prompt: Under SA 710, in the corresponding figures approach, the auditor's opinion:
options: Refers to the current period only
Refers only to the prior period
questions.explanation: Corresponding figures are part of the current period financial statements, so the opinion refers to the current period only, though an unresolved prior-period modification may affect it.

questions.prompt: What is the appropriate opinion given the unrecorded inventory write-down of ₹3.2 crore?
options: Qualified, as the misstatement is material but not pervasive
Adverse, as any refusal by management is pervasive
questions.explanation: ₹3.2 crore exceeds materiality of ₹1.5 crore but is confined to inventory and is about 11% of profit before tax, so it is material but not pervasive. SA 705 requires a qualified opinion.

questions.prompt: How should revenue recognition on distributor rebates and the inventory matter appear in the report?
options: Both as KAMs in the KAM section
Revenue as a KAM; inventory in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section, with a reference in the KAM section
Both in the Emphasis of Matter paragraph
Inventory as KAM; revenue in Other Matter
questions.explanation: Revenue was of most significance and communicated to TCWG, so it is a KAM. A matter giving rise to a modified opinion is described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section, not as a KAM, but the KAM section refers to it.

questions.prompt: Which CARO 2020 clause requires reporting on the unspent CSR of ₹1.1 crore for an ongoing project?
questions.explanation: Clause (xx) covers unspent CSR amounts: for ongoing projects, whether the amount was transferred to the Unspent CSR Account within the time allowed under section 135(6); for others, transfer to a Schedule VII fund.

questions.prompt: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph modifies the auditor's opinion.
questions.explanation: SA 706 states that an EOM paragraph does not modify the opinion; the report states that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter.

questions.prompt: The statement in the Board's report on inventory valuation is a matter for the auditor under SA 720, and if uncorrected it is described in the Other Information section of the auditor's report.
questions.explanation: The Board's report is other information. A material inconsistency with the financial statements that management refuses to correct is described in the 'Information Other than the Financial Statements and Auditor's Report Thereon' section.

questions.prompt: Which conditions must ALL be met for a private company to be exempt from CARO 2020 under the small private company exemption? Select all that apply.
options: Not a holding or subsidiary company of a public company
Paid-up capital and reserves and surplus not more than ₹1 crore as on the balance sheet date
Borrowings from banks or financial institutions not more than ₹1 crore at any time during the year
Total revenue not more than ₹10 crore during the year
Not listed on a stock exchange outside India
questions.explanation: All four conditions must be met. The fifth option is not a condition under the order.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: CARO 2020 does not apply to the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements except clause (___) of paragraph 3.
questions.explanation: Clause (xxi) requires the auditor of the parent to report qualifications or adverse remarks in the CARO reports of companies included in the consolidated financial statements.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'Since the going concern uncertainty is adequately disclosed, the auditor of a listed company should report it as a Key Audit Matter.'
questions.answer:
Not correct.

- A material uncertainty related to going concern is by its nature a KAM, but SA 701 requires it to be reported under SA 570 in a separate section headed 'Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern'.
- The KAM section refers to the MURGC section but does not describe it as a KAM.
- The opinion remains unmodified if disclosure is adequate.

Conclusion: report in the MURGC section with a reference in the KAM section.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between an Emphasis of Matter paragraph and an Other Matter paragraph with examples.
questions.answer:
| Basis | Emphasis of Matter | Other Matter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Refers to | A matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements | A matter not presented or disclosed in the financial statements |
| Purpose | Draws attention to something fundamental to users' understanding of the financial statements | Relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the report |
| Examples | Major catastrophe, uncertainty on outcome of exceptional litigation, early application of a new standard | Prior year audited by predecessor, use of other auditors' work under SA 600, restriction on distribution |
| Effect on opinion | None | None |

Neither is used for a matter that is a KAM, and an EOM cannot replace a required modification.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'Shubh Pvt Ltd has paid-up capital and reserves of ₹80 lakh, no borrowings and revenue of ₹12 crore. CARO 2020 does not apply because its net worth is below ₹1 crore.'
questions.answer:
Not correct.

- The small private company exemption under CARO 2020 requires all conditions to be met cumulatively: not a holding or subsidiary of a public company; paid-up capital plus reserves and surplus not more than ₹1 crore; borrowings from banks or financial institutions not more than ₹1 crore at any time during the year; and total revenue not more than ₹10 crore during the year.
- Shubh Pvt Ltd's revenue of ₹12 crore exceeds ₹10 crore.
- Unless it is a small company or one person company under the Act, CARO 2020 applies.

Conclusion: CARO 2020 applies, subject to checking the small company definition.

questions.prompt: What does the auditor report under clause (vii) of paragraph 3 of CARO 2020?
questions.answer:
- Whether the company is regular in depositing undisputed statutory dues (GST, PF, ESI, income-tax, customs, cess and others) with the appropriate authorities; if not, the extent of arrears outstanding as at the last day of the year for more than six months from the date they became payable.
- Where statutory dues have not been deposited on account of any dispute, the amounts involved and the forum where the dispute is pending.
- The auditor uses records, returns, assessment orders and inquiries, and reports in a tabular form showing nature of statute, nature of dues, amount, period and forum.

chapters.title: Specialised Areas: Special Purpose Audits, Reviews and Related Services
chapters.summary: Audits under special purpose frameworks and of single statements or summaries (SA 800, 805, 810), review engagements (SRE 2400, 2410), prospective financial information (SAE 3400) and agreed-upon procedures (SRS 4400).
chapters.applicableFor: May 2027 onward (ICAI new scheme, CA Final Paper 3)
chapters.lawAsOf: SA 800, 805, 810, SRE 2400, SRE 2410, SAE 3400 and SRS 4400 as issued by ICAI; SEBI LODR Regulation 33 for limited review of quarterly results

lesson.heading: SA 800, SA 805 and SA 810
lesson.body:
**SA 800 (special purpose frameworks)**: financial statements prepared for a specific purpose, for example under a contract's financial reporting provisions, a regulator's format, or a tax or cash basis.

- The auditor understands the purpose, intended users and steps taken by management to decide that the framework is acceptable.
- The report includes an **Emphasis of Matter** paragraph alerting users that the financial statements are prepared under a special purpose framework and may not be suitable for another purpose. The auditor may also restrict distribution or use.

**SA 805 (single financial statements and specific elements, accounts or items)**: for example only the balance sheet, a schedule of receivables, or royalties payable.

- Materiality is set in relation to that statement or element, so it is usually lower than for the full financial statements.
- The auditor considers interrelated items; for example auditing receivables requires attention to revenue cut-off.
- If the opinion on the complete financial statements is adverse or a disclaimer, the auditor does not include an unmodified opinion on a single element in the same report.

**SA 810 (summary financial statements)**: the auditor expresses an opinion on whether the summary is consistent, in all material respects, with the audited financial statements (or is a fair summary), in accordance with the applied criteria. The auditor accepts only if he audited the underlying financial statements.

lesson.heading: Review engagements: SRE 2400 and SRE 2410
lesson.body:
| Basis | SRE 2400 | SRE 2410 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subject | Review of historical financial statements | Review of interim financial information |
| Practitioner | A practitioner who is not the entity's auditor | The independent auditor of the entity |
| Procedures | Mainly inquiry and analytical procedures | Inquiry and analytical procedures, using knowledge from the annual audit |
| Assurance | Limited (moderate) | Limited |
| Conclusion | Expressed in negative form: 'nothing has come to our attention that causes us to believe...' | Same negative form |
| Common use | Bank requirement for a review of a private company's accounts | Limited review of quarterly results of listed entities under SEBI LODR Regulation 33 |

A review is not an audit: it does not involve tests of controls, inspection, observation or confirmation as standard procedures. If the practitioner becomes aware of a matter suggesting material misstatement, he performs additional procedures.

lesson.heading: SAE 3400: prospective financial information
lesson.body:
Prospective financial information (PFI) is based on assumptions about future events and possible actions.

- **Forecast**: prepared on the basis of **best-estimate assumptions** of events management expects to take place.
- **Projection**: prepared on **hypothetical assumptions** about future events and actions that are not necessarily expected (for example a start-up or a major change), or a mix of best-estimate and hypothetical assumptions.

The report under SAE 3400 contains:

- A statement of **negative assurance** on the reasonableness of the assumptions (nothing has come to attention that the assumptions do not provide a reasonable basis).
- An **opinion** that the PFI is properly prepared on the basis of the assumptions and presented in accordance with the framework.
- A caveat that actual results are likely to differ, since anticipated events frequently do not occur as expected.
- For projections, a caution that the PFI is prepared for a stated purpose using hypothetical assumptions.

The auditor should not accept, or should withdraw from, an engagement where assumptions are clearly unrealistic or the PFI will be inappropriate for its intended use. The Code of Ethics (Clause (3) of Part I of the Second Schedule) prohibits a CA from permitting his name to be used with estimates of earnings in a way that leads users to believe he vouches for their accuracy.

lesson.heading: SRS 4400 agreed-upon procedures and related services
lesson.body:
Under **SRS 4400** the auditor performs procedures agreed with the entity and any appropriate third parties and reports **factual findings**.

- **No assurance** is expressed; users draw their own conclusions.
- The report is restricted to the parties that agreed to the procedures.
- Independence is not a requirement under SRS 4400 unless the terms or objective require it; if the auditor is not independent, the report states so.
- The report lists the procedures performed and the findings, including details of errors and exceptions.

Related services also include **compilation engagements (SRS 4410)**, where the practitioner uses accounting expertise to collect, classify and summarise information, with no assurance.

| Engagement | Assurance | Form of report |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Audit | Reasonable (high) | Positive opinion |
| Review | Limited | Negative conclusion |
| Agreed-upon procedures | None | Factual findings |
| Compilation | None | Identification of information compiled |

keyPoints: SA 800 report includes an EOM alerting users to the special purpose framework; distribution may be restricted.
SA 805 materiality is set for the single statement or element; consider interrelated items.
SRE 2400: review by a practitioner who is not the auditor; SRE 2410: review of interim information by the entity's auditor (SEBI LODR Regulation 33 limited review).
SAE 3400: forecast = best-estimate assumptions; projection = hypothetical assumptions; negative assurance on assumptions plus opinion on preparation.
SRS 4400: factual findings, no assurance, restricted use; independence not required unless terms demand it.
Assurance levels: audit reasonable, review limited, AUP and compilation none.

cases.title: Case: Pristine Infra Ltd
cases.body:
CA Meera Kulkarni's firm is the statutory auditor of Pristine Infra Ltd, a listed company. In October 2026 the company makes four requests:

| Request | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| R1 | Limited review of results for the quarter ended 30 September 2026 for filing with the stock exchanges |
| R2 | Report on projected cash flows for a new airport project for 2027-2032, to be submitted to a consortium of banks; the project has not started |
| R3 | Procedures on royalty receipts from a licensee: agree each receipt to bank statements and to the agreement rate, and report what was found |
| R4 | An audit opinion on a statement of receipts and payments for a grant, prepared under the grant agreement's cash basis, for the grant-giving body |

questions.prompt: An auditor's report under SA 800 on financial statements prepared under a special purpose framework must include:
options: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph alerting users to the basis of accounting
questions.explanation: SA 800 requires an EOM paragraph stating that the financial statements are prepared under a special purpose framework and may not be suitable for another purpose.

questions.prompt: The conclusion in a review engagement under SRE 2400 is expressed as:
options: A positive opinion: 'give a true and fair view'
Negative assurance: 'nothing has come to our attention that causes us to believe...'
questions.explanation: A review provides limited assurance, so the conclusion is in negative form.

questions.prompt: Prospective financial information based on best-estimate assumptions of events management expects to occur is called a:
questions.explanation: SAE 3400 defines a forecast as PFI prepared on best-estimate assumptions. A projection uses hypothetical assumptions.

questions.prompt: Under SA 805, materiality for an audit of a schedule of trade receivables is set:
options: At the same amount as for the complete financial statements
In relation to the schedule of receivables itself
questions.explanation: SA 805 requires materiality to be determined for the single statement or element being reported on, which is usually lower than materiality for the full financial statements.

questions.prompt: Which standard governs R1, the limited review of quarterly results?
questions.explanation: SRE 2410 covers review of interim financial information performed by the independent auditor of the entity, which fits a limited review of quarterly results by the statutory auditor.

questions.prompt: The R2 cash flows for a project that has not started are best described as:
options: A forecast, needing a positive opinion on achievability
A projection, with negative assurance on assumptions, an opinion on proper preparation and a caveat that actual results may differ
questions.explanation: A new project depends on hypothetical assumptions, so it is a projection under SAE 3400. The auditor never opines that the results will be achieved.

questions.prompt: R3 should be performed as which kind of engagement, with what output?
options: Audit under SA 805 with an opinion
Agreed-upon procedures under SRS 4400 with a report of factual findings
Review under SRE 2400 with negative assurance
questions.explanation: The company specifies the procedures and wants a report of what was found. This is an AUP engagement with factual findings, no assurance, restricted to the parties that agreed.

questions.prompt: Under SRS 4400, the auditor expresses limited assurance on the subject matter.
questions.explanation: An agreed-upon procedures engagement gives no assurance. The auditor reports factual findings and users draw their own conclusions.

questions.prompt: R4 is an audit under SA 800, and the report should alert users that the statement is prepared on the grant agreement's cash basis and may not be suitable for other purposes.
questions.explanation: A cash-basis statement prepared under a grant agreement is a special purpose framework, so SA 800 applies with an EOM alerting users to the basis of accounting.

questions.prompt: Which elements does an SAE 3400 report on prospective financial information include? Select all that apply.
options: Negative assurance on whether the assumptions provide a reasonable basis
Opinion on whether the PFI is properly prepared on the basis of the assumptions
Caveat that actual results are likely to differ
Opinion that the forecast results will be achieved
questions.explanation: SAE 3400 gives negative assurance on assumptions, a positive opinion on preparation and presentation, and a caveat on achievability. The auditor never guarantees achievability or gives reasonable assurance on assumptions.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the Standard on Related Services for compilation engagements is SRS ___.
questions.explanation: SRS 4410 deals with compilation engagements; SRS 4400 deals with agreed-upon procedures.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'A CA may certify a company's sales projections for the next three years as accurate, since he has examined the assumptions.'
questions.answer:
Not correct.

- Under SAE 3400, the practitioner gives negative assurance on assumptions and an opinion on proper preparation; he does not vouch for achievability, and the report includes a caveat that actual results are likely to differ.
- Clause (3) of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 makes it professional misconduct to permit his name to be used in connection with an estimate of earnings contingent upon future transactions in a manner that may lead to the belief that he vouches for its accuracy.

Conclusion: he may report under SAE 3400 but must not certify the projections as accurate.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a review engagement and an agreed-upon procedures engagement.
questions.answer:
| Basis | Review (SRE 2400 / 2410) | Agreed-upon procedures (SRS 4400) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Objective | Conclude whether anything suggests material misstatement | Perform procedures agreed with users and report findings |
| Assurance | Limited | None |
| Procedures | Decided by the practitioner, mainly inquiry and analytics | Decided by agreement with the engaging parties |
| Report | Negative-form conclusion | Factual findings |
| Distribution | General | Restricted to parties that agreed |
| Independence | Required | Not required unless terms require; state if not independent |

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'The auditor issued a disclaimer of opinion on the complete financial statements of Raga Ltd. He can issue, in the same report, an unmodified opinion on the trade receivables balance under SA 805.'
questions.answer:
Not correct.

- SA 805 states that where the auditor expresses an adverse opinion or disclaims an opinion on the complete set of financial statements, he shall not include in the same report an unmodified opinion on a single financial statement or element that forms part of those financial statements.
- Doing so would contradict the disclaimer and could mislead users.
- An unmodified opinion on a specific element may be expressed only in a separate report, when law permits and the element is not a major portion of the complete financial statements.

Conclusion: not in the same report.

questions.prompt: What should the auditor consider before accepting an engagement to report on summary financial statements under SA 810?
questions.answer:
- SA 810 permits acceptance only if the auditor has been engaged to audit the financial statements from which the summary is derived.
- He determines whether the criteria applied for preparing the summary are acceptable.
- He obtains management's agreement that it will prepare the summary under the criteria, make the audited financial statements available to users without undue difficulty, and include the auditor's report on the summary in any document containing it.
- He agrees the form of opinion: 'consistent in all material respects with the audited financial statements' or 'a fair summary'.
- If the audited financial statements carry a modified opinion, the report on the summary describes it.

chapters.title: Audit of Banks, NBFCs and Public Sector Undertakings
chapters.summary: Bank audits (advances, NPA identification, LFAR), the move to RBI's expected credit loss directions, NBFC audit reporting, and audit of government companies under the C&AG.
chapters.applicableFor: May 2027 onward (ICAI new scheme, CA Final Paper 3)
chapters.lawAsOf: Banking Regulation Act, 1949; RBI prudential norms (IRAC) and RBI ECL directions for commercial banks issued April 2026, effective 1 April 2027; RBI Act section 45-IA; Companies Act, 2013 sections 139(5), 139(7), 143(5)-(7); C&AG (DPC) Act, 1971

lesson.heading: Bank audit: structure and approach
lesson.body:
A bank's financial statements are prepared in the forms in the Third Schedule to the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The audit has two layers:

- **Branch auditors** audit selected branches and report to the central statutory auditors (SA 600 relationship).
- **Central statutory auditors (SCAs)** audit the head office and consolidate branch returns. Their appointment needs RBI approval, and RBI's guidelines prescribe eligibility, tenure, rotation and the number of joint auditors.

Key areas: advances (the largest and riskiest), investments (classification and valuation), deposits, inter-office and suspense accounts, off-balance-sheet items (guarantees, letters of credit), and compliance with RBI directions (KYC, CRR and SLR, exposure norms).

In addition to the main report, the SCA submits a **Long Form Audit Report (LFAR)** in RBI's prescribed format, covering matters such as asset quality, credit monitoring, internal control and compliance. Branch auditors submit branch LFARs.

lesson.heading: Advances and NPA identification
lesson.body:
Audit of advances covers sanction and documentation, drawing power against stock statements, end-use monitoring, security valuation, and asset classification.

A loan becomes a **non-performing asset (NPA)** when:

| Facility | NPA when |
| --- | --- |
| Term loan | Interest or principal instalment remains overdue for more than 90 days |
| Cash credit or overdraft | Account remains **out of order** for more than 90 days |
| Bills purchased and discounted | Bill remains overdue for more than 90 days |
| Short-duration crop loan | Instalment or interest overdue for two crop seasons |
| Long-duration crop loan | Instalment or interest overdue for one crop season |

Out of order: outstanding balance continuously above the sanctioned limit or drawing power for 90 days; or, where within limits, no credits continuously for 90 days, or credits not enough to cover interest debited during the same period.

Classification under the IRAC norms: **substandard** (NPA for up to 12 months), **doubtful** (substandard for 12 months; D1 up to 1 year in doubtful, D2 1 to 3 years, D3 more than 3 years), **loss** (identified as uncollectible). Interest on NPAs is not recognised as income until realised.

**RBI's ECL framework**: RBI issued final directions in April 2026 moving scheduled commercial banks (other than regional rural banks, small finance banks and payments banks) to an expected credit loss approach with Stage 1, 2 and 3 assets from **1 April 2027**, with transition relief for the existing book. Stage 3 broadly corresponds to credit-impaired (NPA) assets. Check the ICAI study material and RBI website for what is examinable in your attempt; provisioning percentages are not tested here.

lesson.heading: NBFC audit
lesson.body:
- Every NBFC must hold a certificate of registration from RBI under **section 45-IA of the RBI Act, 1934** and meet the net owned fund requirement.
- RBI's scale-based regulation places NBFCs in Base, Middle, Upper and Top layers with progressively stricter norms.
- Under RBI's directions on the auditor's report for NBFCs, the auditor submits a separate report to the Board covering matters such as: whether the company is registered; whether it meets the **principal business criteria** (financial assets more than 50% of total assets and income from financial assets more than 50% of gross income); compliance with prudential norms on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning; and, for deposit-taking NBFCs, compliance on deposits. Exceptions are reported to RBI.
- CARO 2020 clause (xvi) asks whether the company is required to be registered under section 45-IA and whether it has conducted non-banking financial activities without registration.
- NBFCs required to follow Ind AS apply the Ind AS 109 expected credit loss model, alongside RBI's prudential floors.

lesson.heading: Audit of public sector undertakings and the C&AG
lesson.body:
The Comptroller and Auditor General of India (C&AG) is a constitutional authority (Articles 148 to 151). The C&AG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 sets out its duties.

For **government companies** (section 2(45): at least 51% of paid-up share capital held by the Central or State Government or both):

| Provision | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Section 139(5) | C&AG appoints the statutory auditor within 180 days from the start of the financial year |
| Section 139(7) | First auditor appointed by C&AG within 60 days of registration |
| Section 143(5) | C&AG directs the manner of audit; auditor reports on the directions and action taken, and submits a copy of the report to C&AG |
| Section 143(6) | C&AG may conduct a supplementary audit within 60 days of receiving the audit report, and comment on or supplement the report |
| Section 143(7) | C&AG may order a test audit |

Types of audit in the public sector:

- **Propriety audit**: whether expenditure meets standards of financial propriety, for example not more than the occasion demands, not for private benefit.
- **Performance audit**: whether programmes achieve objectives with economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
- **Comprehensive audit**: a broad appraisal of the performance of public sector enterprises.

keyPoints: Term loan NPA: overdue more than 90 days; CC/OD: out of order more than 90 days; crop loans: two seasons (short) or one season (long).
Substandard up to 12 months as NPA; doubtful D1/D2/D3 by time in doubtful; loss when uncollectible; no income on NPAs until realised.
RBI ECL directions for scheduled commercial banks apply from 1 April 2027 (Stages 1, 2, 3).
NBFC: registration under section 45-IA; principal business criteria 50% assets and 50% income; separate auditor's report to the Board.
Government company audit: C&AG appoints within 180 days (s.139(5)) or 60 days for first auditor (s.139(7)); directions u/s 143(5); supplementary audit within 60 days u/s 143(6).
Public sector audits: propriety, performance (economy, efficiency, effectiveness), comprehensive.

cases.title: Case: Ganga Bank, Varanasi branch
cases.body:
CA Rohit Verma is the branch auditor of the Varanasi branch of Ganga Bank for the year ended 31 March 2026. Selected accounts:

| Account | Facility | Status at 31 March 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P | Term loan | Instalment due on 15 January 2026 unpaid (75 days overdue) |
| Q | Cash credit, limit ₹50,00,000 | Balance continuously above drawing power since 20 November 2025 (131 days) |
| R | Term loan | Classified NPA on 31 January 2025; still unpaid |
| S | Short-duration crop loan | Overdue for one crop season |
| T | Cash credit within limit | Credits during the last 90 days cover the interest debited |

The branch has credited interest of ₹2,40,000 on account Q to income for the quarter ended 31 March 2026, though nothing was received.

questions.prompt: A term loan becomes an NPA when interest or principal instalment remains overdue for:
questions.explanation: RBI's prudential norms treat a term loan as NPA when any amount of interest or principal remains overdue for more than 90 days.

questions.prompt: Under section 139(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, the auditor of an existing government company is appointed by:
options: The C&AG, within 180 days from the commencement of the financial year
questions.explanation: For government companies, the C&AG appoints the auditor within 180 days from the start of the financial year.

questions.prompt: Under section 143(6), the C&AG may conduct a supplementary audit of a government company within:
options: 30 days of receipt of the audit report
60 days of receipt of the audit report
questions.explanation: Section 143(6)(a) allows the C&AG to conduct a supplementary audit within 60 days from the date of receipt of the audit report.

questions.prompt: Which test does an NBFC's auditor apply to check the principal business criteria?
options: Financial assets more than 50% of total assets and income from financial assets more than 50% of gross income
Net owned fund more than ₹100 crore
Loans more than 75% of total assets
questions.explanation: RBI's 50-50 test: financial assets must exceed 50% of total assets and income from financial assets must exceed 50% of gross income.

questions.prompt: How should account R be classified at 31 March 2026?
questions.explanation: R became NPA on 31 January 2025. It stays substandard for 12 months (to 31 January 2026) and is then doubtful. At 31 March 2026 it has been doubtful for about 2 months, which is D1 (up to 1 year).

questions.prompt: What should Rohit do about the ₹2,40,000 interest on account Q?
options: Accept it, since interest accrued under the loan agreement
Require reversal: Q is an NPA (out of order more than 90 days) and interest on NPAs is recognised only when realised
questions.explanation: Q has been above drawing power continuously for 131 days, so it is out of order and an NPA. Income on NPAs is not recognised until actually received, so the unrealised interest must be reversed.

questions.prompt: Which accounts are NPAs at 31 March 2026?
questions.explanation: P is 75 days overdue (not more than 90). S is overdue for one crop season (short-duration crops need two). T has credits covering interest, so it is not out of order. Q (131 days) and R are NPAs.

questions.prompt: RBI's ECL directions for scheduled commercial banks issued in April 2026 take effect from 1 April 2027.
questions.explanation: RBI's final directions move eligible scheduled commercial banks from incurred loss to expected credit loss from 1 April 2027, with transition relief for the existing book.

questions.prompt: Account T is out of order because it is a cash credit account and the borrower has not repaid the principal.
questions.explanation: A CC account within limits is out of order only if there are no credits for 90 days or credits are not enough to cover interest debited. T's credits cover interest, so it is regular.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are audits commonly carried out in the public sector under the C&AG? Select all that apply.
options: Tax audit under the Income-tax Act
questions.explanation: Propriety, performance and comprehensive audits are characteristic of government audit. AUP and tax audit are not C&AG audit types.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: an NBFC must obtain a certificate of registration from RBI under section ___ of the RBI Act, 1934.
questions.explanation: Section 45-IA requires registration and net owned fund before an NBFC commences or carries on business.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'A cash credit account in which the balance has always been within the drawing power can never become an NPA.'
questions.answer:
Not correct.

- A CC or OD account is an NPA if it remains out of order for more than 90 days.
- Out of order covers two situations: (a) the outstanding balance remains continuously above the sanctioned limit or drawing power for 90 days; or (b) where the balance is within the limit, there are no credits continuously for 90 days as on the balance sheet date, or credits are not enough to cover the interest debited during the same period.
- So an account within the drawing power can still be out of order under (b).
- Drawing power based on stock statements older than prescribed limits also raises an irregularity issue.

Conclusion: such an account can become an NPA.

questions.prompt: Explain the role of the C&AG in the audit of a government company under the Companies Act, 2013.
questions.answer:
- Section 139(5): appoints the statutory auditor within 180 days of the start of the financial year; section 139(7): first auditor within 60 days of registration (if C&AG fails, the Board appoints within 30 days, and so on).
- Section 143(5): issues directions on the manner of audit; the auditor reports on directions, action taken and impact on accounts, and submits a copy of the report to the C&AG.
- Section 143(6): may conduct a supplementary audit within 60 days of receiving the report and comment on or supplement it; comments are sent to the company and placed before the AGM with the audit report.
- Section 143(7): may order a test audit, with the report laid before Parliament or the State Legislature where applicable.
- The C&AG also conducts propriety and performance audits under the DPC Act, 1971.

questions.prompt: What special areas does a central statutory auditor examine in a bank audit beyond those in a company audit?
questions.answer:
- Classification of advances into standard and NPAs and adequacy of provisions under RBI norms (and the ECL framework from 1 April 2027 for eligible banks).
- Income recognition: reversal of unrealised interest on NPAs.
- Investments: classification and valuation as per RBI directions.
- Inter-office (inter-branch) reconciliation and old unreconciled entries; suspense and sundry accounts.
- Off-balance-sheet exposures: guarantees, letters of credit, derivatives.
- Compliance with CRR, SLR, capital adequacy disclosures, exposure norms and KYC.
- Consolidation of branch returns and reliance on branch auditors (SA 600).
- The Long Form Audit Report in RBI's format and other certificates required by RBI.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'Tejas Finance Pvt Ltd lends money as its main business but has not registered with RBI, as its auditor need not report this.'
questions.answer:
Not correct.

- Section 45-IA of the RBI Act, 1934 requires an NBFC to obtain a certificate of registration before commencing or carrying on non-banking financial business.
- CARO 2020 clause (xvi) requires the auditor to report whether the company is required to be registered under section 45-IA and, if so, whether registration has been obtained, and whether it has conducted NBFC activities without a valid certificate.
- Under RBI's directions on the auditor's report for NBFCs, the auditor reports to the Board and, where the company fails the principal business criteria or is unregistered, reports exceptions to RBI.

Conclusion: the auditor must report the non-registration.

resources.title: Comptroller and Auditor General of India

chapters.title: Internal Audit, Due Diligence, Forensic Accounting and BRSR Assurance
chapters.summary: Internal audit under section 138, management and operational audit, due diligence, investigation and forensic accounting, and assurance on sustainability reporting (BRSR and BRSR Core).
chapters.applicableFor: May 2027 onward (ICAI new scheme, CA Final Paper 3)
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies Act, 2013 section 138 with Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014; ICAI Standards on Internal Audit and Forensic Accounting and Investigation Standards; SEBI LODR Regulation 34(2)(f) and SEBI BRSR Core circulars of July 2023 and March 2025

lesson.heading: Internal audit
lesson.body:
Section 138 read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 requires the following to appoint an internal auditor:

| Class | Threshold (preceding financial year) |
| --- | --- |
| Listed company | Always |
| Unlisted public company | Paid-up share capital ₹50 crore or more; or turnover ₹200 crore or more; or outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions above ₹100 crore at any time; or outstanding deposits ₹25 crore or more at any time |
| Private company | Turnover ₹200 crore or more; or outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions above ₹100 crore at any time |

The internal auditor is a chartered accountant or cost accountant (in practice or not) or another professional decided by the Board, and may or may not be an employee. Under section 144, the statutory auditor cannot provide internal audit services to the company, its holding or subsidiary.

ICAI's Internal Audit Standards Board issues **Standards on Internal Audit (SIAs)**. Internal audit covers risk management, governance and internal control, and gives assurance and advisory input to the audit committee.

**Management audit** evaluates the effectiveness of management in achieving objectives (planning, organising, decision-making). **Operational audit** reviews operations for economy, efficiency and effectiveness (for example procurement cycle times, idle capacity).

lesson.heading: Due diligence
lesson.body:
Due diligence is an investigation of a business before a transaction such as an acquisition, merger, investment or lending, to confirm facts and find hidden risks.

Types: financial, tax, legal, commercial, operational, HR, environmental and IT.

A financial due diligence report typically covers:

- Quality of earnings: normalised EBITDA after removing one-off and non-recurring items.
- Net assets: adjustments for overstated assets and unrecorded liabilities.
- Net debt and debt-like items: unpaid statutory dues, gratuity shortfall, deferred consideration.
- Working capital trends and seasonality.
- **Hidden liabilities**: guarantees, pending litigation, tax demands, environmental obligations, undisclosed related party arrangements.

Due diligence is not an audit: the scope is agreed with the client, and the output is findings that feed the price, deal structure, warranties and indemnities.

lesson.heading: Investigation and forensic accounting
lesson.body:
| Basis | Audit | Investigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Objective | Opinion on financial statements | Establish facts on a specific matter |
| Scope | Set by law and SAs | Set by the client or authority |
| Period | Usually one year | Can cover several years |
| Evidence | Sufficient appropriate for reasonable assurance | As needed to prove or disprove allegations |
| Approach | Assumes no suspicion | Begins with suspicion |

**Forensic accounting** applies accounting, auditing and investigative skills to produce evidence fit for legal proceedings. ICAI has issued **Forensic Accounting and Investigation Standards (FAIS)** for members doing such engagements.

Techniques:

- Fraud triangle: pressure, opportunity and rationalisation.
- Data analytics: Benford's law on first digits, duplicate payments, vendor-employee address or bank account matches, round-sum and weekend entries.
- Document examination, interviews, background checks and asset tracing.
- Chain of custody for digital and documentary evidence, so it is admissible.

The practitioner reports facts and findings; whether a person is guilty is for the courts to decide.

lesson.heading: Sustainability reporting and BRSR assurance
lesson.body:
Under SEBI LODR Regulation 34(2)(f), the **top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation** include a **Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR)** in the annual report. It is organised around the nine principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct.

**BRSR Core** is a subset of key ESG indicators (for example greenhouse gas emissions, water, energy, waste, employee well-being, gender diversity, inclusive development and openness of business) for which SEBI's July 2023 circular introduced **reasonable assurance** on a glide path by market capitalisation, starting with the top 150 listed entities.

SEBI's circular of 28 March 2025 eased the framework: a listed entity may obtain either **assurance** or an **assessment** of BRSR Core, and value chain disclosures and their assessment or assurance were made voluntary for a period. SEBI has also stated that the assurance provider need not be a chartered accountant.

ICAI's Sustainability Reporting Standards Board has issued standards on sustainability assurance, including **SSAE 3000, Assurance Engagements on Sustainability Information**. The practitioner applies independence and quality control, plans based on materiality of ESG metrics, tests data collection systems and source records, and reports either a reasonable assurance opinion (positive form) or a limited assurance conclusion (negative form).

keyPoints: Section 138: listed companies always; unlisted public: paid-up ≥ ₹50 crore, turnover ≥ ₹200 crore, borrowings > ₹100 crore or deposits ≥ ₹25 crore; private: turnover ≥ ₹200 crore or borrowings > ₹100 crore.
Section 144 bars the statutory auditor from providing internal audit services to the company, its holding or subsidiary.
Due diligence: quality of earnings, net debt, hidden liabilities; findings affect price and warranties.
Investigation starts with suspicion, has client-defined scope and may cover several years; audit gives an opinion on financial statements.
BRSR mandatory for top 1,000 listed entities; BRSR Core assurance or assessment per SEBI circulars of July 2023 and March 2025.
Reasonable assurance = positive opinion; limited assurance = negative conclusion.

cases.title: Case: Northstar Logistics Pvt Ltd
cases.body:
Arya Capital plans to acquire 100% of Northstar Logistics Pvt Ltd (turnover ₹240 crore, bank borrowings ₹60 crore). It appoints CA Vikram Joshi's firm for financial due diligence. Findings so far:

| Item | Finding |
| --- | --- |
| EBITDA | Reported ₹32 crore includes a one-time insurance claim of ₹4 crore |
| Guarantee | Northstar guaranteed a ₹15 crore loan of a promoter-owned company; not disclosed in notes |
| Tax | Income-tax demand of ₹6 crore under appeal, disclosed as contingent liability |
| Vendors | Three transport vendors share a bank account number with a purchase manager's relative |
| Internal audit | No internal auditor has been appointed |

The buyer asks Vikram's firm to also investigate the vendor matter.

questions.prompt: Under Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014, a private company must appoint an internal auditor if, in the preceding financial year, it had:
options: Paid-up capital of ₹50 crore or more
questions.explanation: For private companies the tests are turnover of ₹200 crore or more, or outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions exceeding ₹100 crore at any time. The paid-up capital and deposit tests apply to unlisted public companies.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes investigation from audit?
options: Investigation always covers one financial year
Investigation begins with suspicion and its scope is set by the client or authority
Investigation gives an opinion on true and fair view
questions.explanation: An investigation is a fact-finding exercise on a specific matter, usually triggered by suspicion, with scope defined by the person appointing the investigator.

questions.prompt: Under SEBI LODR Regulation 34(2)(f), BRSR is required for:
options: Top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation
questions.explanation: BRSR is mandatory for the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a common data analytics test in a forensic engagement on payments?
options: Benford's law analysis of first digits of invoice amounts
Confirming share capital with the RTA
questions.explanation: Benford's law compares the actual first-digit distribution with the expected one; unusual patterns can indicate fabricated amounts.

questions.prompt: For quality of earnings, what normalised EBITDA should the due diligence report present?
questions.explanation: The one-time insurance claim of ₹4 crore is non-recurring and is removed: ₹32 crore - ₹4 crore = ₹28 crore.

questions.prompt: How should the undisclosed ₹15 crore guarantee be reported in the due diligence?
options: Ignore it, as it is not on the balance sheet
As a hidden liability and related party exposure affecting price, warranties and indemnities
questions.explanation: Undisclosed guarantees for promoter entities are classic hidden liabilities. Due diligence flags them so the buyer can adjust price or seek indemnities or release of the guarantee.

questions.prompt: Is Northstar Logistics Pvt Ltd required to appoint an internal auditor under section 138?
options: No, private companies are never covered
Yes, because turnover of ₹240 crore is ₹200 crore or more
No, because borrowings are below ₹100 crore
questions.explanation: A private company with turnover of ₹200 crore or more in the preceding year must appoint an internal auditor. Either test is enough, so the borrowing level does not matter.

questions.prompt: SEBI has clarified that the assurance provider for BRSR Core need not be a chartered accountant.
questions.explanation: SEBI treats BRSR Core assurance as profession-agnostic, subject to the provider having the necessary expertise and no conflict of interest.

questions.prompt: In the vendor investigation, Vikram's firm should state in its report that the purchase manager is guilty of fraud.
questions.explanation: A forensic practitioner reports facts and findings supported by evidence (shared bank accounts, payment trails). Deciding guilt is for the courts or the appropriate authority.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are elements of the fraud triangle? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The fraud triangle has pressure, opportunity and rationalisation. Segregation of duties is a control that reduces opportunity.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: section ___ of the Companies Act, 2013 prohibits the statutory auditor from rendering internal audit services to the company.
questions.explanation: Section 144 lists prohibited services, including internal audit, accounting and bookkeeping, and management services.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'Due diligence is just another name for an audit of the target's financial statements.'
questions.answer:
Not correct.

- An audit gives an opinion on whether financial statements are true and fair, under SAs and law, usually for one year.
- Due diligence is an investigation before a transaction, with scope agreed with the client, covering several periods and areas beyond accounts (tax, legal, commercial, HR, IT).
- It focuses on quality of earnings, net debt, working capital and hidden liabilities such as guarantees, litigation and tax demands.
- The output is findings and risks to feed the price, structure and contractual protections, not an audit opinion.

Conclusion: they differ in objective, scope and output.

questions.prompt: Explain the BRSR Core assurance framework and the role of a practitioner.
questions.answer:
- BRSR under SEBI LODR Regulation 34(2)(f) applies to the top 1,000 listed entities; BRSR Core is a set of key ESG indicators within it.
- SEBI's July 2023 circular introduced reasonable assurance of BRSR Core on a glide path by market capitalisation, starting with the top 150 entities.
- SEBI's March 2025 circular allowed entities to choose assurance or assessment of BRSR Core, and relaxed value chain requirements.
- The provider need not be a CA but must be independent and competent.
- A CA performing it applies ICAI's sustainability assurance standards (such as SSAE 3000), quality control and independence, understands data systems, tests source records and estimates, and reports a reasonable assurance opinion or limited assurance conclusion.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'The statutory auditor of Alpha Ltd can also be appointed as its internal auditor, as that will save costs.'
questions.answer:
Not correct.

- Section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013 prohibits an auditor from rendering internal audit services, directly or indirectly, to the company, its holding company or subsidiary.
- Section 138 and Rule 13 allow the Board to appoint a CA, cost accountant or other professional as internal auditor, but not the statutory auditor.
- The restriction protects independence: the statutory auditor would otherwise review his own work (self-review threat).

Conclusion: the appointment is not permitted regardless of cost.

questions.prompt: What steps should a forensic accountant follow when investigating suspected vendor kickbacks?
questions.answer:
- Agree scope, objective and reporting lines in writing; check independence and competence.
- Secure evidence early: preserve ERP data, emails and documents with a chain of custody.
- Run analytics on the vendor master and payments: shared bank accounts, addresses or PANs with employees and relatives, duplicate invoices, price variances, round amounts, approvals just below limits.
- Examine documents: contracts, rate approvals, GRNs, delivery evidence.
- Interview relevant staff in a planned sequence, after document review.
- Trace funds where legally possible.
- Report facts and findings with evidence, without concluding on guilt, and recommend control improvements.

chapters.title: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
chapters.summary: Professional misconduct under the Schedules to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, the disciplinary mechanism, the Code of Ethics, auditors' liabilities under the Companies Act, 2013, and NFRA basics.
chapters.applicableFor: May 2027 onward (ICAI new scheme, CA Final Paper 3)
chapters.lawAsOf: Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 as amended by the CA, CWA and CS (Amendment) Act, 2022; ICAI Code of Ethics; Companies Act, 2013 sections 132, 140, 141, 143, 144 and 147; NFRA Rules, 2018

lesson.heading: The Schedules: what counts as misconduct
lesson.body:
The Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 has two Schedules.

**First Schedule** (less serious, handled by the Board of Discipline):

- Part I: members in practice. Key clauses:

| Clause | Misconduct |
| --- | --- |
| (1) | Allows a non-member to practise in his name |
| (2) | Shares fees or profits with a non-member |
| (4) | Enters into partnership with a non-member (other than as permitted) |
| (6) | Solicits clients or professional work by circular, advertisement, personal communication or interview |
| (7) | Advertises professional attainments or services (except as permitted by Council guidelines) |
| (8) | Accepts a position as auditor previously held by another CA without first communicating with him **in writing** |
| (9) | Accepts appointment as auditor of a company without first ascertaining that the requirements of the Companies Act on appointment have been complied with |
| (10) | Charges fees based on a percentage of profits or contingent on findings (except as permitted) |
| (11) | Engages in any business or occupation other than the profession, unless permitted by the Council |
| (12) | Allows a person not a member, or a member not his partner, to sign on his behalf |

- Part II: members in service; Part III: members generally; Part IV: other misconduct (for example conviction or conduct bringing disrepute).

**Second Schedule** (more serious, handled by the Disciplinary Committee). Part I, members in practice:

| Clause | Misconduct |
| --- | --- |
| (1) | Discloses client information without consent or legal requirement |
| (2) | Certifies or reports without examining the records |
| (3) | Permits his name to be used with estimates of earnings so as to vouch for their accuracy |
| (4) | Expresses an opinion on financial statements of a business in which he, his firm or a partner has a substantial interest |
| (5) | Fails to disclose a material fact known to him that is not disclosed in the financial statements |
| (6) | Fails to report a material misstatement known to him |
| (7) | Does not exercise due diligence, or is grossly negligent |
| (8) | Fails to obtain sufficient information to warrant the expression of an opinion |
| (9) | Fails to invite attention to a material departure from generally accepted audit procedures |
| (10) | Fails to keep client money in a separate bank account |

lesson.heading: Disciplinary mechanism and the Code of Ethics
lesson.body:
- An information or complaint goes to the **Director (Discipline)**, who forms a prima facie opinion.
- If the member is prima facie guilty of misconduct in the **First Schedule**, the matter goes to the **Board of Discipline**; if in the **Second Schedule** or both, to the **Disciplinary Committee**.
- Penalties include reprimand, removal of name from the Register for a period, and fine. The 2022 amendment raised the fine limits and brought registered firms within the disciplinary mechanism; check the current amounts in the Act before quoting them.

**Code of Ethics** (issued by ICAI) points examined often:

- Communication with the previous auditor must be in writing, by a mode that gives proof of delivery (registered post acknowledgement due, hand delivery with acknowledgement, or email with proof of delivery). Mere posting under certificate of posting is not enough.
- Council guidelines limit tax audit assignments a member may accept in a financial year under section 44AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (or its equivalent in the Income-tax Act, 2025).
- Website and certain forms of publicity are allowed within ICAI's advertisement guidelines; soliciting work is not.
- Fees based on a percentage of profits are prohibited except where permitted (for example receivers or liquidators, where fees may be based on a percentage of realisation).

lesson.heading: Liabilities under the Companies Act, 2013
lesson.body:
| Provision | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Section 141(3) | Disqualifications: for example holding securities of the company, indebtedness above ₹5 lakh, business relationship, relative a director or KMP, full-time employment elsewhere, more than 20 company audits |
| Section 144 | Prohibited non-audit services: accounting, bookkeeping, internal audit, design of financial information systems, actuarial, investment advisory, investment banking, outsourced financial services, management services |
| Section 140(5) | The Tribunal may order a change of auditor if he acted fraudulently or colluded in fraud; such auditor cannot be appointed by any company for 5 years |
| Section 143(12) | Duty to report fraud by officers or employees |
| Section 147(2) | Auditor contravening sections 139, 143, 144 or 145: fine ₹25,000 to ₹5 lakh, or four times the remuneration, whichever is less; if knowingly or wilfully with intention to deceive, imprisonment up to 1 year and fine ₹1 lakh to ₹25 lakh |
| Section 147(3) | Refund of remuneration and damages to the company, statutory bodies or others for loss arising from incorrect or misleading statements in the report |

Civil liability also arises for negligence under the general law of contract and tort; criminal liability under section 447 for fraud and for false statements in a prospectus.

lesson.heading: NFRA basics
lesson.body:
The **National Financial Reporting Authority** is set up under **section 132** of the Companies Act, 2013. Its functions: recommend accounting and auditing standards for approval by the Central Government, monitor and enforce compliance, oversee the quality of service of professionals, and investigate professional or other misconduct.

Under the NFRA Rules, 2018 it covers auditors of, among others:

- Companies whose securities are listed in India or outside India.
- Unlisted public companies with paid-up capital of at least ₹500 crore, or annual turnover of at least ₹1,000 crore, or aggregate outstanding loans, debentures and deposits of at least ₹500 crore as on 31 March of the preceding year.
- Insurance companies, banking companies, and companies engaged in generation or supply of electricity.
- Bodies corporate referred by the Central Government in the public interest.

On proof of misconduct, NFRA may impose under section 132(4): a penalty of not less than ₹1 lakh, extendable to five times the fees received, for individuals; not less than ₹10 lakh, extendable to ten times the fees received, for firms; and debar the member or firm from practice for a period of six months to ten years. Where NFRA has initiated an investigation, ICAI cannot proceed on the same matter.

keyPoints: First Schedule (Board of Discipline): e.g. Part I clauses (6) soliciting, (7) advertising, (8) no written communication with previous auditor, (9) not ascertaining compliance on appointment, (10) contingent fees.
Second Schedule (Disciplinary Committee): e.g. Part I clauses (1) disclosure of information, (5)-(6) failure to disclose or report, (7) gross negligence, (8) insufficient information.
Communication with the previous auditor: in writing with proof of delivery.
Section 147(2): fine ₹25,000 to ₹5 lakh or four times remuneration (lower); wilful: up to 1 year plus ₹1 lakh to ₹25 lakh.
NFRA (s.132): individuals min ₹1 lakh up to 5x fees; firms min ₹10 lakh up to 10x fees; debarment 6 months to 10 years.
NFRA coverage: listed companies; unlisted public companies with paid-up ≥ ₹500 crore, turnover ≥ ₹1,000 crore or loans, debentures and deposits ≥ ₹500 crore; banks, insurers, electricity companies.

cases.title: Case: CA Ravi Bansal
cases.body:
CA Ravi Bansal is a partner of Bansal Gupta and Co., Jaipur. Events during 2026:

| Ref | Event |
| --- | --- |
| E1 | Appointed auditor of Shree Cement Traders Ltd in place of CA Anil; sent a letter to Anil by ordinary post under certificate of posting and started work the next day |
| E2 | Agreed with a client that his fee for a GST refund claim would be 10% of the refund sanctioned |
| E3 | While auditing Rupa Steels Ltd, learnt that the company had not recorded a ₹2 crore penalty order received before the year end; he signed an unqualified report without mentioning it |
| E4 | Allowed his article assistant to sign tax audit reports when he was travelling |
| E5 | Holds 50 equity shares of Rupa Steels Ltd, a listed company with turnover of ₹1,400 crore |

questions.prompt: A complaint alleges misconduct only under the First Schedule. After the Director (Discipline) finds the member prima facie guilty, the matter goes to:
questions.explanation: First Schedule matters go to the Board of Discipline. Second Schedule matters, or both Schedules, go to the Disciplinary Committee.

questions.prompt: NFRA is constituted under which section of the Companies Act, 2013?
questions.explanation: Section 132 provides for the constitution, powers and functions of the National Financial Reporting Authority.

questions.prompt: Under section 132(4), the maximum monetary penalty NFRA may impose on an audit firm for professional misconduct is:
questions.explanation: For firms, the penalty is not less than ₹10 lakh and may extend to ten times the fees received. For individuals it is not less than ₹1 lakh and may extend to five times the fees.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a prohibited service under section 144 for a statutory auditor?
options: Design and implementation of a financial information system
Representation before tax authorities in an assessment
questions.explanation: Section 144 lists accounting, internal audit, design of financial information systems, actuarial, investment advisory, investment banking, outsourced financial and management services. Tax representation is not in the list.

questions.prompt: Event E1 amounts to misconduct under:
options: Clause (8) of Part I of the First Schedule, as communication must be in writing with proof of delivery
Clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule
No misconduct, since a letter was posted
questions.explanation: Clause (8) requires prior communication in writing with the previous auditor. ICAI's Code of Ethics requires proof of delivery; a certificate of posting is not enough.

questions.prompt: Event E3 is professional misconduct under:
options: Second Schedule, Part I, clauses (5) and (6)
questions.explanation: Failing to disclose a material fact known to him and failing to report a material misstatement known to him are covered by clauses (5) and (6) of Part I of the Second Schedule.

questions.prompt: Regarding E5, what is the position of Ravi Bansal under section 141(3) of the Companies Act, 2013?
options: No issue, since 50 shares is a trivial holding
He is disqualified from being auditor of Rupa Steels Ltd, as a person holding any security of the company is disqualified
He can continue if he discloses the holding in the report
questions.explanation: Section 141(3)(d)(i) disqualifies a person who, or whose relative or partner, holds any security of or interest in the company. For the auditor himself any holding disqualifies (the ₹1 lakh face value relaxation applies only to relatives).

questions.prompt: Under section 147(2), an auditor who wilfully contravenes section 143 with intention to deceive may be punished with imprisonment for up to one year and a fine of ₹1 lakh to ₹25 lakh.
questions.explanation: Section 147(2) provides the higher punishment where contravention is knowing or wilful with intention to deceive the company, its shareholders, creditors or tax authorities.

questions.prompt: Event E4 is professional misconduct under clause (12) of Part I of the First Schedule.
questions.explanation: Clause (12) prohibits allowing a person who is not a member, or a member who is not his partner, to sign on his behalf or on behalf of his firm any balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statement.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are covered by Part I of the Second Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949? Select all that apply.
options: Gross negligence in the conduct of professional duties
Charging fees as a percentage of profits
questions.explanation: Gross negligence (clause 7), disclosure of information (clause 1) and certifying without examination (clause 2) are Second Schedule misconduct. Soliciting and percentage fees are First Schedule, Part I clauses (6) and (10).

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: under section 140(5), an auditor removed by order of the Tribunal for acting fraudulently is not eligible to be appointed as auditor of any company for ___ years.
questions.explanation: The proviso to section 140(5) bars such an auditor from appointment for five years from the date of the Tribunal's final order.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: CA Ravi agreed that his fee for a GST refund claim would be 10% of the refund sanctioned (E2).
questions.answer:
Ravi is guilty of professional misconduct.

- Clause (10) of Part I of the First Schedule prohibits a member in practice from charging or offering to charge, accepting or offering to accept, fees based on a percentage of profits or contingent upon findings or results of such employment, except as permitted by Council regulations.
- Regulation 192 of the CA Regulations, 1988 permits percentage fees only in specified cases, such as receivers or liquidators (on realisation), and a refund claim is not one of them.
- A fee depending on the refund sanctioned is a contingent fee.

Conclusion: misconduct under clause (10), dealt with by the Board of Discipline.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'CA Meena, auditor of a listed company, posted the audit findings on her social media page to show her expertise, without naming the client but describing the industry and city.'
questions.answer:
Meena is guilty of professional misconduct.

- Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule prohibits disclosing information acquired in the course of professional engagement to any person other than the client, without consent or as required by law.
- If the client can be identified from the industry and city, this is a disclosure of confidential information.
- Posting to show expertise may also amount to advertising or soliciting under clauses (6) and (7) of Part I of the First Schedule.
- For a listed company, NFRA has jurisdiction over professional misconduct of its auditor under section 132.

Conclusion: misconduct; the matter may be examined by NFRA or ICAI as applicable.

questions.prompt: Explain the functions and powers of NFRA and the auditors it covers.
questions.answer:
- Constituted under section 132 of the Companies Act, 2013.
- Functions: recommend accounting and auditing standards to the Central Government; monitor and enforce compliance with them; oversee the quality of service of the professions; protect the public interest.
- Coverage under the NFRA Rules, 2018: auditors of listed companies (in or outside India); unlisted public companies with paid-up capital ≥ ₹500 crore, turnover ≥ ₹1,000 crore, or loans, debentures and deposits ≥ ₹500 crore; insurance, banking and electricity companies; and bodies referred in public interest.
- Powers: investigate professional misconduct; powers of a civil court; once it starts an investigation, ICAI cannot proceed on the same matter.
- Penalties under section 132(4): individuals not less than ₹1 lakh up to 5 times fees; firms not less than ₹10 lakh up to 10 times fees; debarment for 6 months to 10 years.
- Appeals lie to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'CA Neeraj accepted the audit of Delta Ltd after receiving the appointment letter, without checking whether the company had passed the resolution required under the Companies Act.'
questions.answer:
Neeraj is guilty of professional misconduct.

- Clause (9) of Part I of the First Schedule makes it misconduct for a member in practice to accept an appointment as auditor of a company without first ascertaining from it whether the requirements of the Companies Act relating to appointment (now sections 139 and 140, and section 141 eligibility) have been complied with.
- An appointment letter alone does not show that the members' resolution, the eligibility certificate and consent, or the procedure for removal or non-reappointment of the previous auditor were followed.
- He should have examined the resolution and related compliance before accepting.

Conclusion: misconduct under clause (9), dealt with by the Board of Discipline.
